stories.headline: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 8: WR trade for Chiefs? Goff for MVP?
stories.summary: Get ready for Week 8 with takes on the Chiefs' trade deadline plan, Jared Goff's sneaky season, Kevin Stefanski's Coach of the Year case and the Ravens' struggling defense.
stories.body:
Are you excited for NFL Week 8? This is our first loaded slate of the season. Ravens at Bills. Vikings at Lions. Browns at Steelers. Chiefs at Broncos. Bears at Seahawks. Even the not-so-great games (Falcons at Buccaneers and Colts at Jaguars) mean a lot for divisional standings.

Every Tuesday of the NFL season, I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide'

This week, I'll start with a prediction/plea for the Chiefs to make a trade for a receiver. Then I'll put all my hope and joy on the back of a fourth-round rookie. And finally, I'll admit I can't do my job.

Jump to:

Chiefs will make a WR trade

Stefanski will be Coach of the Year

Goff is a sleeper MVP candidate

Coleman could save Broncos' offense

Ravens' D disqualifies them from contention

QB3 Leonard starts for Colts by Week 10

Young is a complicated study

Some extra inklings

I think ... the Chiefs' loss to Seattle will bully them into making the trade they need to make
Have you ever gotten embarrassed on national television? Me neither.

The 2026 Chiefs sure have. Kansas City scored three points against the Seahawks on Sunday night, marking only the second time in Patrick Mahomes' career that his team has been held to three or fewer points. The 11 first downs the Chiefs accumulated were their fewest in 153 Mahomes starts, and this was only his fourth start without a single explosive pass. The offense averaged 4.3 yards per play (148th out of 153), produced minus-0.13 EPA per play (148th) and had a success rate of 34% (152nd).

It's easy to explain this one. The Seahawks, off a two-game losing streak, were hosting an unbeaten Chiefs team at home -- that defense was amped-up for four quarters. The Chiefs were down both starting tackles (Josh Simmons and Jaylon Moore) along with two of three starting receivers (Tyquan Thornton and Rashee Rice), and the passing offense played like it. Even the Chiefs' ace in the hole -- their interior offensive line's dominance in the running game -- was beaten in this game, as they ran into the league-best defensive tackle duo of Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy II. I didn't think it would look as bad as it did, but it's not too surprising it fell to such dramatic pieces.

Let's also consider the larger context. Simmons didn't just miss this game -- he has been out all season, and ESPN reported Sunday that Reid and Mahomes had to kick Simmons out of a meeting last Wednesday after frustrations boiled over. He has missed the entire season because of back issues, has recently been placed on injured reserve and missed time last season for personal reasons and a wrist injury. Rice has now missed 27 of the 43 games he could have played since the start of the 2024 season for injury or suspension. It's not just that the Chiefs' star receiver and early-drafted left tackle missed this past week -- it's that they've proven to be consistently unavailable. Meanwhile, Chiefs' first-round receiver Xavier Worthy dropped another pass in Week 7 as he continues to be unusable on most downfield routes.

This was a one-off in that the Chiefs were dramatically outmanned and should get some of these players back from the medical tent soon. But this was not a one-off in the sense that Rice, Simmons and Worthy are just unreliable players.

The Chiefs should clearly consider drastic measures. Undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has played well enough in Simmons' absence that there's no need to make a big trade for a left tackle. But the need for a three-down receiver who can endure a large target volume and succeed at all three levels of the field is glaring. Worthy isn't even the best speed receiver on the team when Thornton is healthy, so I think Worthy should be dangled in trade packages as well -- he has more value in theory right now than he does in practice.

Whether the Chiefs actually will consider a big deadline trade is less clear. General manager Brett Veach has typically been active around the deadline, executing at least one in-season trade in five consecutive seasons from 2020 to 2024 before going quiet in 2025. The biggest such deal was the future third-round pick traded for Kadarius Toney in 2022. The Chiefs had just traded Tyreek Hill in the 2022 offseason and were looking for speed on offense. Toney didn't hit as a receiver, but he provided a big punt return in the Chiefs' Super Bowl victory that season.

This Chiefs team (5-1) is as well suited for a postseason run as that Chiefs team (5-2 at the time of the trade). Through seven weeks of the 2026 season, the Chiefs are fifth in offensive EPA per play and fourth in defensive EPA per play. They are ninth in offensive points per drive and third in defensive points per drive. With an actual running game well in hand and a reinvigorated defense, this is as balanced of a Chiefs team as I can remember. They just need some more juice on offense.

ESPN's Adam Schefter has reported as such. From "The Pat McAfee Show" on Monday: "They have been calling around, and I don't think it would be a surprise to see them continue to attempt to add a wide receiver before the trade deadline."

I have five deadline deals for a receiver in mind. These are not sourced and were first written down on the back of a napkin. It's very likely the other teams in these hypotheticals would not even listen to deals for their wideouts. Do not yell at me on the internet about these trade proposals.

1. Send Worthy and a 2027 third-round pick to the Jaguars for Brian Thomas Jr.

Jacksonville benched Thomas in the second half of its Week 6 game. The only value the Jaguars were getting from him was theoretical field stretching -- Worthy can do much the same, and Mahomes and the Chiefs can give Thomas a chance to rediscover his 2024 form in a new zip code.

2. Send a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 conditional fifth-round pick to the Cowboys for George Pickens.

The Cowboys have 2025 trade acquisition Pickens and 2026 trade acquisition Joey Porter Jr. playing on contract years, and it's hard to imagine they extend both ex-Steelers at market rates. If Pickens would recoup a third-round compensatory pick in free agency, the Chiefs can sweeten the pot with a future pick conditional on production levels and give the Cowboys their third-round comp pick without having to manipulate the formula this offseason. How the Cowboys play in Weeks 8 and 9 (vs. Cardinals, at Colts) will have a big impact here.

3. Send a 2027 fourth-round pick to the Eagles for Dontayvion Wicks.

If I were the Chiefs, I'd be putting a first and then some on the table for DeVonta Smith. It absolutely would not work -- Eagles GM Howie Roseman isn't going to trade both A.J. Brown and Smith in the same season -- but you have to try as the Eagles stare down the barrel of a rebuild in 2027. In lieu of Smith, Wicks has all the traits of a three-level receiver -- ball tracking, ability to catch away from his frame, burst, size -- without any of the route or hands consistency. Grab him for a Day 3 pick and hope to run hot!

4. Send Worthy and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Saints for Devaughn Vele and a 2027 sixth-round pick.

Before you laugh, that's tied-for-22nd-in-total-receptions Devaughn Vele to you! Vele is an entirely unexciting target, but he is also basically what the Chiefs need. He's a big-bodied receiver who can take a ton of contact and endure 10-plus-target games. He also makes good catches away from his frame and provides red zone value -- something the Chiefs' worryingly undersized receiver room has always failed to bring. With Jordyn Tyson coming back from a hamstring injury at some point and the Saints' season on life support, New Orleans can take the gamble on rehabilitating Worthy.

5. Send Worthy, a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 third-round pick to Jets for Garrett Wilson.

Of all the untouchable star receivers on losing football teams (Nico Collins on the 2-5 Texans, Smith on the 2-5 Eagles, etc.), Wilson is the one I can maybe see moving within the next two weeks. Jets GM Darren Mougey seems so secure in his reputation as a wheeler-and-dealer that the fanbase would forgive him for moving Wilson should the Jets fire Aaron Glenn and go scorched earth before the deadline. The one issue? The Jets are already loaded in the first round of the 2027 draft with two additional Day 1 picks. Does Mougey really need more capital? It's less than a 1% chance ... but greater than a 0% chance.

I think ... Kevin Stefanski should win Coach of the Year
Three coaches in NFL history have won the AP Coach of the Year award at least three times: Don Shula (3.5, as he shared a win in 1967), Bill Belichick (three) and Chuck Knox (three). I think Stefanski should become the fourth this season.

That's right. For those who forgot, Stefanski won Coach of the Year twice in his six-year tenure with the Browns. In 2020, his first season at the helm, Stefanski infused Baker Mayfield with hitherto unseen playmaking and went 11-5 -- heck, he even won a playoff game in Cleveland. Three years later, Stefanski's 2023 Browns went 11-6 despite splitting the regular season across five starting QBs (Deshaun Watson, Dorian Thompson-Robinson, PJ Walker, Jeff Driskel and Joe Flacco). If a leap year comes once every four years, then a Stefanski COTY win is an every-three-years event, because it's 2026 and the man is doing it again.

The Falcons are 3-4 through seven games with a big win over the previously undefeated 49ers this past Sunday. And when starting quarterback Michael Penix Jr. is active, they're 3-2. More impressive than the record is the quick evolution Penix has undergone under Stefanski and offensive coordinator Tommy Rees. For the previous two seasons under Falcons offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, Penix rarely left the pocket and aggressively pushed the ball downfield. He played quarterback much like a trebuchet might: He just sat there and launched the sucker.

Stefanski's offense has precipitated a different style of play from Penix, who is getting rid of the ball remarkably faster than he did in his first two seasons as a pro and operating closer to the line of scrimmage. Where Penix once never moved, he's now leading the league in designed rollout rate, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

Coaches don't win awards because they successfully shepherd young quarterbacks to stylistic changes, but it's worth stating clearly that this is not easy to do. Most young QBs don't change their stripes. They might improve or decline, but they do so within the same play style. Bo Nix is playing the same style of ball in 2026 (while struggling) as he did in 2025 (while excelling). The same was true for Drake Maye from 2024 into 2025. Even Caleb Williams, who has undergone a serious metamorphosis under Ben Johnson, is mostly grafting skills onto the same existing base of a high-creativity play style.

That the Falcons have readily gotten Penix to think about football in a different fashion altogether is impressive. Doubly impressive is how Stefanski has this passing game operating in the context of his rushing attack. The Falcons, with Stefanski's longtime partner-in-crime Bill Callahan coaching the offensive line, have one of the league's best rushing attacks (sixth in rushing yards per game, 139.9), and they lean on it like no other. Since Penix returned to the starting lineup, no team has a higher called run rate than Atlanta (46.5%).

Surely the Falcons run a ton of play-action then, right? And they must hunt deep shots off that established run? Wrong. Penix has a 26.8% play-action rate on the season, 14th among league passers (league average is 24.6%). And on play-action dropbacks, he has a depth of target of 7.1 -- below the league average of 7.7.

Stefanski and Rees have been careful about giving Penix too much runway on play-action deep shots because of the QB's warts. He's a highly inconsistent player for downfield accuracy and particularly struggles when pressured. While play-action can slow down an effective pass rush, it can also quickly create protection busts. The quarterbacks who benefit the most from play-action are hyper-precise anticipation throwers who can quickly expose a linebacker one step out of alignment. Penix has that caliber of release speed and velocity but hugely lacks the necessary accuracy -- especially on downfield throws.

Instead, the Falcons use the boot game to get Penix free-access completions for yards after the catch instead of deep opportunities for explosives -- 53% of his yards have come after the catch this season, up from 47% in 2025 and 37% in 2024. Save for Bijan Robinson, the Falcons' pass catchers -- Drake London, Kyle Pitts Sr., Jahan Dotson, Charlie Woerner, etc. -- aren't really known for their after-the-catch ability. This is all scheme, baby. When we remove running back targets, the disparity grows even more, as 47% of Penix's yards this season are from YAC, relative to 32% and 30% in the two previous seasons.

Stefanski won this award in 2020 for what he got from Mayfield and in 2023 for how he scrabbled together a quarterback room. Ideally, we would learn to give this award for reasons beyond quarterbacking. But here, Stefanski still wins. His running game is getting the best out of Robinson that we've ever seen. Stefanski retained incumbent defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich and has reaped the rewards with an aggressive, high-pressure unit despite subpar talent. Stefanski is not a perfect fourth-down decision-maker or clock manager, but he's one of the league's better coaches in both fields.

Funny enough, if not Stefanski for the award, I'd like to see his successor in Cleveland win it. Todd Monken inherited Stefanski's team and has gotten big production out of young players. The Browns are 5-2 despite poor quarterback play. The co-excellence of Monken and Stefanski serves as a nice reminder that splits are sometimes necessary. Cleveland needed a new voice, and Stefanski needed a new room to speak in. Both parties are better off for their split.

The Falcons are well positioned in a weak NFC South to take a division title. Even with the 49ers' injuries considered, Atlanta has plenty of proof it can play with anyone in this league. Ending the season 10-7 with a home playoff game feels like the winning ticket. Whether or not that's enough for Stefanski to win his third Coach of the Year recognition, he deserves his flowers in this space. I love the job he's doing in Atlanta.

I think ... Jared Goff is the sleeper MVP nobody's talking about
The Lions are 4-2 after a 20-17 win over the Packers. It finally seemed like a manageable game for the Lions, rather than a desperate second-half sprint to keep pace with an opposing offense that the Detroit defense had no prayer of stopping. Detroit now hosts another division rival, the undefeated Vikings, with the potential to hand them their first loss and pull closer to pole position in the highly competitive NFC North. If the Lions win that game, they'll be 5-2 and the Vikings would be 6-1. And Goff likely would have had a good day against the vaunted Brian Flores defense.

Through six weeks, Goff has 150 completions on 223 attempts (67.3% completion rate). His passer rating of 112.5 is second only to Ravens QB Lamar Jackson. His total dropback EPA of 58.5 is just barely behind Josh Allen (58.6) for the league lead. He has thrown 14 touchdown passes and no interceptions, which ties 2019 Russell Wilson for the most touchdowns in a six-game, interception-free start to a season in NFL history.

That Goff hasn't thrown an interception despite how often the Lions have been stuck in shootout game scripts is eye-popping. He has also been one of the least-pressured quarterbacks (30.8%, fifth lowest among high-volume passers). At first, that sounds like a disqualifying characteristic for an MVP, but 49ers QB Brock Purdy has the lowest pressure rate and Allen is sixth. High-performing quarterbacks benefit from good pass protection and also make the sort of plays that mitigate pressures altogether.

This is where Goff has really impressed -- he's playing with an excellent rhythm. Here's a good example on a nice play design. The Lions bluff the screen to running back Jahmyr Gibbs, and Goff wants tight end Brock Wright (89) on the vertical. But a spiking defensive end collapses Goff's throwing platform. No biggie ... Goff resets with quick feet and dumps the ball to Gibbs instead of trying to force a late throw to Wright along the sideline.

I love the rhythm and comfort with which Goff is playing this season -- this, more than anything, seems reminiscent of the Ben Johnson era and what was absent in the brief John Morton intermission last season. Drew Petzing and the improvements along the entire Lions offensive line have Goff playing with urgency but control -- comfort without laziness. Goff will never be an extended-play maven, and that lack of rushing production will always narrow his path to an MVP award. But on pure pass attempts -- no scrambles, no sacks, no nothing -- Goff has collected 82.2 EPA through six games. Jaguars QB Trevor Lawrence is second at 59.6.

I took a quick peak at the MVP odds and found Goff eighth behind Allen (makes sense), Purdy (makes sense), Joe Burrow (makes sense), Lawrence (I agree), Mahomes (ehhh), Maye (probably not) and Williams (missed too many games). Goff has barely better odds than Packers quarterback Jordan Love despite the head-to-head win. The next closest player? Gibbs.

There's almost no shot that Gibbs wins the MVP over Goff if Detroit's season runs out with an NFC North title. The Lions are a fairly balanced offense (15th in overall pass rate, 11th in pass rate over expectation). For a running back to win the MVP over a quarterback, the production and talent disparity would have to be so obvious -- think Robinson vs. Penix -- that it would be a farce to select otherwise. Until proven otherwise, MVP is a quarterback award in the modern era.

Goff is far from a favorite at this stage, and rightfully so. Burrow is the one throwing the ball on every down, and the Bengals have the easiest schedule left. The AFC North, at least by record, is as competitive as the NFC North. If you're making me guess today who will actually win the award at the end of the season, I think I'd take Burrow.

But if the question is which player could emerge from the void of hype-less-ness and become a favorite by December, Goff seems like the obvious choice.

I think ... Jonah Coleman is coming to save the Broncos' offense
OK, that might be a little much. But hear me out.

The Broncos' rookie running back has the juice. On 19 carries this season, he's averaging 4.9 yards -- J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey are at 3.4 and 3.6, respectively. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Coleman has generated 17 more rushing yards than expected (Dobbins is at minus-77; Harvey is at minus-34) and has four more first downs than expected -- for a total of seven on just 19 carries!

Nine of those carries came in his Week 7 return from injury against the Cardinals (2-5); he had missed the past four weeks because of an ankle sprain. He had as many carries as Dobbins and Harvey combined and took 50% of the snaps overall (Dobbins at 21%; Harvey at 25%). Coleman added two catches on just six routes for a 11-touch, 69-yard day. Coach Sean Payton said, "Got to get him more touches."

I agree.

We've spent so much time worrying about quarterback Bo Nix and the passing game in Denver -- which, by the way, was far from fixed but also a little improved on Sunday -- that we've barely spoken about the running game. Through the first six weeks of the season, the Broncos were averaging 3.5 yards per carry on running back runs (fifth worst), and it didn't seem like the offensive line's fault. In fact, Broncos running backs were averaging 1.2 yards before contact per carry -- above the league average.

The Denver backs had 99 fewer rushing yards than expected per Next Gen Stats' modeling (third worst) because Harvey and Dobbins are incomplete players. Harvey lacks feel and vision behind an offensive line and is best used in space as a pass catcher. Dobbins, who has the ideal mental traits for a running back, lacks the athletic pop to actually make plays in tight spaces.

The lack of any running game hurt the overall health of the Broncos' offense, as there was nowhere to hide the passing game's struggles when the rushing attack also failed to carry its own weight. Denver has a good enough defense to win with a methodical philosophy on offense, but when Nix produces a haphazard outing, the running game has been incapable of steadying the offensive heartbeat.

It's never really good news when a fourth-round rookie returning from early-season injury is considered the bringer of stability to an offense -- Denver never should have let it get this far. But even before the injury, when Harvey and Dobbins were hurt in Week 2 against the Jaguars, Coleman salted the game away in the four-minute offense over veteran back Tyler Badie. It speaks to a level of trust that Payton has in him, and deservedly so. Coleman is quick in mind and in body -- he explodes into the hole and finishes through contact. He's no Bijan Robinson, but he's the best between-the-tackles ball carrier I've seen wear a Broncos uniform this season.

Denver is hosting a rematch with the Chiefs on Sunday (4:25 p.m. ET, CBS). Remember, these two teams played Week 1 on "Monday Night Football" when we didn't yet know what we were getting from Kenneth Walker III and the new-look Chiefs offense. Now, Denver is 5-2 -- only a half-game back from the 5-1 Chiefs -- and needs to protect Nix from the high-pressure game plan that defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo deployed the last time around. The best way to slow down the pass rush? Run the ball.

A reliable running game would go a long way as the Broncos continue figuring out how to insulate Nix and restore his confidence as a thrower -- a reliable and occasionally explosive running game would go twice as long. If Denver has an improved offensive performance against the Chiefs this week, many will cite Payton on the headset as the difference. But I won't be surprised if it's Coleman toting the rock that swings things the other way.

I think ... the Ravens' pass defense disqualifies them as a contender
Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow had a perfect passer rating (158.3) in the second half against the Ravens on Sunday. He is the first quarterback since Josh Allen in the 2024 wild-card round to post a perfect passer rating in the second half (minimum 15 dropbacks). Burrow's success rate (88.9%, 16-of-18 on dropbacks) was the best since 2016 Dak Prescott in Week 11 against ... the Ravens.

It's spooky how often the Ravens find themselves on the wrong side of these stats. Baltimore's first three losses of the season have all come in games in which it once led by 10-plus points, making it the sixth team in NFL history to do that. The most recent is the 2022 Ravens.

In that the Ravens have surrendered three multiscore leads, I'm not venturing far into hyperbole when I say there's something wrong with their pass defense. In likely dropback situations -- that is, when leading in the second half -- a defense should be able to get to more exotic calls and rush the passer more ambitiously. According to Next Gen Stats, the Ravens are 29th in completion percentage surrendered (64.8%) and 26th in yards per attempt allowed (7.8) on plays with a pass probability of at least 75% (accounting for down-and-distance, score differential, etc.).

The issue is explicitly in coverage, not pass rush. Baltimore is getting enough pressure in obvious passing situations (42%, above league average) but is entirely unable to close on routes. On these obvious passing downs, 40% are thrown to "open" receivers with at least 3 yards of separation, the third-highest rate in the NFL, according to Next Gen Stats charting.

Why can't the Ravens play stickier coverage? Well, they are a zone-heavy team under Jesse Minter, and they remain so in clear passing downs (61% zone coverage, 12th among defenses). Baltimore doesn't really have the personnel to play man coverage across the board. No. 2 cornerback Marlon Humphrey is 30 years old and doesn't have the same speed he once did. Behind him, the Ravens are cycling through options over the slot. Keyon Martin was the leading No. 3 corner with 14 snaps, taking the mantle from rookie Chandler Rivers, who was outsnapping him a few weeks ago.

Here's a third-and-3 in man coverage in the third quarter against Cincinnati on Sunday. Baltimore leaves top corner Nate Wiggins locked with Bengals receiver Tee Higgins to the top of the screen, and Wiggins aggressively plays the fade route, keeping upfield and outside positioning on Higgins. He's acting as if he has help inside -- but linebacker Roquan Smith immediately snaps his head to Bengals No. 1 receiver Ja'Marr Chase on the opposite side of the formation, and deep safety Kyle Hamilton is too far out of position to impact the catch point. First down to Higgins.

Here's another man coverage snap -- this one in the red zone. Here, the Ravens explicitly double Chase with Humphrey and safety Malaki Starks. They aggressively gave Humphrey help in this game, a testament to their uncertainty around his play in matchups like this one. Hamilton ends up responsible for Higgins on the bender, and like Wiggins on the previous play, he gets aggressive outside positioning. Hamilton thinks he has help from someone -- maybe Smith down the hashes, Starks as a center-fielding safety -- but doesn't. It's another easy Higgins completion and leaves a frustrated trio of defenders talking things out in the end zone when the play is done.

A healthy fear of Chase created serious spacing issues for Baltimore across the board. Watch the weight of Chase on the in-breaker pull linebacker Trenton Simpson deep downfield, which makes the quick checkdown to Erick All Jr. that much more profitable. And then one drive later, watch Chase on the same curl route pull defenders downhill and open up so much space for Higgins to break into the sideline behind him.

It's tough to overly fault safety K'Von Wallace, who's in for the injured Jaylinn Hawkins and should not be nearly so far downfield here (though Hawkins himself has been a problem in space for much of the season). Hawkins and Starks have both been late to find routes in zone coverage and taken poor angles to get there. Wiggins has struggled with top receivers such as Higgins and the Falcons' Drake London. Hamilton missed a few tackles in this game and drew a costly defensive holding penalty -- his value is never going to be in his downfield coverage. And while Smith is a smart coverage linebacker, he lacks length and the size to impact the catch point, and his quickness is not what it once was.

The collective pool of coverage talent in Baltimore just doesn't move the needle. Were Wiggins a set-it-and-forget-it CB1 worth locking in man coverage on one side of the formation, things would be easier. He's not. Were Humphrey a veteran CB2 who could be trusted against elite receiver duos, things would be easier. He's not. So, when opposing offenses begin collecting dropbacks against Baltimore, they get many bites at a particularly juicy apple. Eventually, they hit on a couple of big plays, and the scoreboard evens.

I'm not sure where salvation comes for Baltimore. About 49% of my brain says Minter is a great defensive coach and the Ravens will become much, much tighter in their zones as the season goes on. Minter's defenses in Los Angeles were notoriously well connected and keyed in on tendency, but the Ravens' group has been the opposite through seven weeks. Those tides can change.

But 51% of my brain says their talent just isn't good enough to make a playoff run through some trio of Allen, Burrow, Drake Maye, Patrick Mahomes and Trevor Lawrence. More time together under Minter will help clean up some spacing issues -- they'll be much better the next time they play the Bengals, I'm sure -- but too many players are making too many mistakes for me to believe in the healing magic of friendship and communication. If the Ravens have to man up anybody right now ... I'm probably picking the other guys to win the down.

The trade deadline is in two weeks, and Minter's old Chargers (who are 0-6) might end up dealing some players. Keep an eye on safety Elijah Molden and cornerback Donte Jackson.

I think ... Riley Leonard will be starting by Week 10
There is no distant rumble on the horizon that more obviously anticipates a quarterback benching than a head coach insisting that no benching is imminent. Asked by reporters for the second consecutive week whether Daniel Jones is still the starting quarterback in Indianapolis, coach Shane Steichen reiterated that, yes, Jones is still the starter.

Here's the thing: Jones wasn't particularly bad on Sunday against the 6-0 Vikings -- at least, not on the scale of his recent play and the expectations for a quarterback going up against Brian Flores' league-leading defense. To be clear, he absolutely was bad -- 13-for-22, 108 yards, an interception, four sacks -- but just not much worse than could be expected.

That, of course, is the problem.

Steichen called a sterilized game Sunday, treating his quarterback less like a trusted playmaker and more like a radioactive isotope. Indianapolis ran the ball heavily -- the Colts had a pass rate over expectation of minus-17.5%, the second-lowest mark of the past two years. Despite all the run-action, the Colts offense went play-action on only 14.8% of their pass attempts, the lowest of any Jones start. This game was equivalent in game plan to the 2025 Philip Rivers start against the Seahawks (minus-23.5% pass rate over expectation; 7.1% play-action rate) -- that's the current esteem to which Steichen holds Jones. He's playing him like 43-year-old Philip Rivers.

Instead, it was all quick game, with one- and three-stop drops in the hope that Jones would get the ball out quickly and avoid the Vikings' ferocious pressure package altogether. Of course, Jones had a few snaps of timely delivery and pristine placement. He also tried to throw two first-half picks and actually did the deed in the fourth quarter. Point-and-shoot quarterbacking rarely works, even for veteran supercomputers such as Rivers. For Jones, a bulky body with good mobility (he still looks spry enough off the Achilles injury) whose career has been more about aggressive throws in the face of pressure ... it was not a winning formula.

Of course, it's not just Jones. The passing attack is absent tight end Tyler Warren and receiver Alec Pierce. No quarterback feels good up against an elite defense in 2026 when Laquon Treadwell and Keenan Allen are running a majority of the routes. Earlier, I excused the Chiefs for their own terrible offensive performance vs. the Seahawks and advocated for wide receiver trades before any larger Patrick Mahomes judgments could be made. I extend that same grace to Jones and the Colts, who are a better passing attack than their 4.9 yards per attempt and minus-0.15 EPA per dropback on Sunday imply.

With the necessary caveats made ... the Colts are going to have to bench Jones. As the 2-5 team stares down a road game in Jacksonville in Week 8, it's looking at the last domino before a full-scale teardown starts in Indianapolis. DeForest Buckner, Cam Bynum, Grover Stewart, Quenton Nelson, Josh Downs, Jonathan Taylor ... there are plenty of quality Colts players worth trading at the deadline.

As Indianapolis punts on 2026 and looks to 2027, figuring out what it has -- if anything -- in its two young backup quarterbacks is critical. The Colts do not have their first-round pick in the 2027 draft -- that belongs to the Jets via the Sauce Gardner trade -- and cannot reasonably consider drafting a potential starter until 2028. Finding a bridge quarterback is high on the laundry list for 2026 objectives should their season functionally end in Jacksonville next week -- a bridge quarterback cheaper than Jones' $46.8 million cap hit in 2027.

A few weeks ago, I predicted we'd see Anthony Richardson Sr. at some point -- he has been dressing as the Colts' No. 2 quarterback with second-year pro Leonard available as the emergency No. 3. Since that prediction, Richardson faces a misdemeanor charge for marijuana possession following a traffic stop earlier this month. While he faces no imminent punishment from the league -- the legal process has yet to play out -- this is the sort of error that shakes up a QB2 depth chart.

Who truly knows what Richardson is capable of after a one-in-a-million eye injury ended his 2025 season during pregame warmups in October? While Richardson has more NFL experience than Leonard by years, he has started only 15 games (Leonard has one), and they're the same age (24). Leonard has the advantage of extra contract years as the Colts look for a bridge starter in 2027; he has two additional seasons of team control after this one, and Richardson is a 2027 free agent.

Either option is a defensible choice, and I demand half-credit for this prediction if the Colts pull Jones for Richardson after their Week 9 game against the Cowboys. I'd lean Leonard because a good Richardson season creates a weird contract decision this offseason. No matter what, if the Colts start dealing assets in the next couple of weeks, I expect a quarterback change to swiftly follow.

I think ... about Bryce Young, but I don't know anything
We're 3½ years into Young's career, and I still don't know exactly how good this guy is. There is no individual player in the league, let alone quarterback, who confounds me the way Bryce Young confounds me. Who are you?!

Let's take the widest view then funnel in. Since 2024 (I'm throwing out 2023 because it was a disastrous season under Frank Reich), Young is one of 31 quarterbacks with at least 600 dropbacks. He is 25th in EPA per dropback and 28th in dropback success rate (Aaron Rodgers, Cam Ward and Joe Flacco are worse). He is 28th in completion percentage and 30th in off-target percentage (only Caleb Williams is worse, and he's going to catch up to Young pretty quickly here).

I think it's easy for people to forget just how bad Young has been on a large sample -- remember, we eliminated his terrible 2023 rookie season. And unlike a lot of the young quarterbacks who have shaky numbers over the past few seasons -- Ward, Tyler Shough, Jayden Daniels, etc. -- Young's bad statistical output is not the result of terrible negative plays drawing his performance down. He is around league average for interception rate and sack rate. The average Young pass just isn't all that valuable. It is not completed often enough, and when it is completed, it doesn't generate enough yardage. It's as simple as that.

Now let's narrow things. We don't really care how Caleb Williams produced in 2024, and for good reason -- he's clearly a different guy than he was then. Drake Maye is different. Justin Herbert is different. The NFL stands for Not For Long; it's concerned only with what you've done lately. So, let's push aside past seasons and take a look at Young's 2026 progress report.

Panthers coach Dave Canales gave offensive coordinator Brad Idzik playcalling responsibilities this season, and there has been a boost in the Panthers' offense accordingly. The second season of reigning Offensive Rookie of the Year Tetairoa McMillan and the third year of Jalen Coker opposite him helps, too. Through seven weeks of the season, Young is still 30th in completion percentage and 33rd in off-target rate among 34 quarterbacks ... but he's balancing the scales with bigger throws. Young is seventh in air yards per attempt, a new single-season best for him. He's 11th in explosive pass rate and 12th in first down/touchdown per dropback rate.

The chief change in the Panthers' offense under Idzik is this: Carolina is not doing too much schematically different, but it has changed the proportions in which it has asked Young to do what he does. When Canales first came to Carolina, the Panthers wanted Young to be a spread-n-shred point guard. In 2024, 22.4% of his dropbacks were in empty formations, then 18.3% in 2025. This season, it's down to 12.8%. As empty has dropped, under center has risen (13.1% to 14.6% to 19.2%) and play-action has followed (22.2% to 25.2% to 27.6%).

The abandonment of empty is particularly interesting when we look at what has replaced it. The Panthers hired Darrell Bevell this offseason as an associate head coach. For the past four years, he served as Mike McDaniel's quarterbacks coach and passing game coordinator in Miami. A huge part of the Panthers' playbook has suddenly become extremely McDaniel-inspired. The Panthers, much like the Dolphins did with Tua Tagovailoa, are weaponizing Young's lightning-quick release and strong pre-snap processing to hit easy-access RPOs.

The fact that Young is experiencing a production bump while enjoying the same dusting of McDaniel magic dust that once inflated Tagovailoa's output is ... suspicious. But Young has something that Tagovailoa never had: the ability to make plays under pressure.

Young's career numbers don't stack up well on all dropbacks, but on pressured dropbacks (again since 2024) he has always had a knack for playmaking without inviting great disaster. Here's that same table from above, but only on pressured dropbacks. Over the past three seasons, Young is now 11th in dropback success rate, 11th in explosive pass rate and 15th in EPA per dropback. Notice again that his sack rate and interception rate remain low relative to his peers.

These are my favorite traits of Young's -- his twitch, his poise and his creativity. It's especially notable in the red zone, where Young flits in and out of tight spaces to manipulate defenders and break coverages. He doesn't make the same truly elite plays out of structure that Josh Allen, Williams and Patrick Mahomes do -- he lacks the arm strength and the physical bulk -- but he is in the tier below.

Young has played well under pressure over a multi-season sample, so he should -- with an improvement to the base offense around him -- be able to sustain a solid passing attack and respectable NFL offense. We've seen it in flashes this season, and we said that last year, too. But it's never consistent and never strung together for more than three consecutive games. Sunday's 43-13 disaster against the Buccaneers was far from Young's fault -- the defense was embarrassed and his offensive line had its worst game of the season against the Bucs' deep stable of powerful rushers -- but Young certainly didn't help. He was erratic and late, as he often is when he gets jittery in the pocket after several hits.

The Panthers are 3-3 and, in theory, in the driver's seat in the NFC South. They have an enormous game at the Packers on Thursday night. Remember, they won at Lambeau Field last season as 13-point underdogs. If Carolina can run the ball well and play deep zone coverages that force Jordan Love to check down the football -- and Green Bay's terrible rushing attack continues -- it has a clear avenue to victory.

The Panthers are capable of beating the Packers and most other contenders on any given Sunday. But they're also capable of losing in dramatic fashion to the one-win Buccaneers. And that's because their quarterback remains a mystery bag even now, 50 starts into his NFL career. I know he's getting better, but I'm not sure he's getting better enough fast enough. I know he can make plays under pressure, but I'm not sure he makes enough big ones. I have one job (literally, this is my job), and I still can't figure out what to do about Bryce Young.

Four things I might think

I might think ... the Buccaneers are back. Tampa Bay has a defensive line full of buttkickers who fold in the pocket on every passing down and a pair of lights-out corners on the outside who can challenge anyone in man-to-man situations. The Buccaneers' defense looked like what I long believed it could this Sunday against the Panthers.

I might think ... Tee Higgins is the 11th-best receiver in football. In no particular order: Ja'Marr Chase, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Justin Jefferson, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb, Drake London, Chris Olave, Nico Collins, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Garrett Wilson. Those are the 10 better than Tee. Zay Flowers, Malik Nabers, A.J. Brown and DeVonta Smith are with him in that next tier.

I might think ... Houston still isn't out of it. Pull a string on my back and I say "Houston's advanced metrics are still pretty good!" Even with the travel back from London, the lookahead to the bye week and the insanely hot game by Giants QB J.J. McCarthy all considered ... it's very embarrassing to lose to the Giants. Still, Houston goes from 2-5 to 5-5 pretty quick. Their next three opponents are at the Chargers (0-6), at the Browns (5-2) and against the Colts (2-5).

I might think ... 18 is a powerful number. The Saints had 18 team rushing yards on 17 carries against the Steelers. Rookie receiver Cyrus Allen led all Chiefs wide receivers with 18 receiving yards vs. the Seahawks. You tell me which stat is more pitiful. (J.J. McCarthy also wears 18 now, and he's twice the man "Nine" ever was).

stories.headline: 2026 World Series odds: Brewers one win away, Rays 15-1 to mount comeback
stories.summary: The World Series schedule, lines and odds to win, including MVP.
stories.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are on the verge of sweeping their second consecutive playoff series to win their first-ever World Series, circumstances that have them as -5000 title favorites coming out of Monday's Game 3. The Tampa Bay Rays are out to 15-1 to mount a comeback that has only ever been accomplished once in an MLB postseason and never in the World Series.

Both teams came into the 2026 regular season as at least relative longshots to win the title, with Milwaukee beginning the campaign at a 14th-best 35-1. Tampa Bay came in at 80-1, which would (if they were to complete an improbable comeback) tie the 1991 Minnesota Twins for the longest preseason underdog to win an MLB title in the last 40 seasons, according to data from SportsOddsHistory.com.

After a four-hit game on Monday, Jackson Chourio has become the odds-on favorite for World Series MVP at -120, with teammate William Contreras not too far behind at +100. Junior Caminero is the only player in the same stratosphere at 40-1... and, once again, that's assuming an historic comeback.

The Brewers are -124 to win Game 4 and finish the job on Tuesday, with the Rays coming in at +103. The over/under is set at 7.

Odds by DraftKings at time of publication.

To win series: Rays 15-1, Brewers -5000

Brewers lead series 3-0

stories.headline: Inside the stunning 72-hour Lakers sale -- and the uncertainty that still looms
stories.summary: Three days of secret talks resulted in Mark Walter flipping the Lakers -- and reignited yet another round of bickering among the six Buss siblings.
stories.body:
BOB IGER WAS on his 213-foot sailing superyacht on Aug. 12, winding down a monthlong vacation in Europe following a historic, two-decade run as CEO of Disney.

The biggest event of the day was supposed to be the first total solar eclipse over the continent in more than a century.

Millions of tourists, including Iger, had booked vacations along the eclipse's path from Greenland to Southern Spain during the syzygy -- a word derived from Ancient Greek for "yoked together" -- which describes a rare astronomical event in which three or more celestial bodies align in a straight line.

During a solar eclipse, the moon sits exactly between the sun and Earth, casting its shadow onto Earth. Some enjoy the rare view -- through special sunglasses.

Others ascribe great meaning and magic to eclipses. As those tourists headed to viewing spots for the solar eclipse across Europe, Iger was in a wholly different syzygy with his longtime friend and business partner Josh Kushner and Los Angeles Lakers owner Mark Walter.

The alignment of three financial heavy hitters was about to turn what should have been a once-in-a-generation event -- last year's record-breaking sale of the Lakers from the Buss family to Walter -- into the NBA's most shocking news -- again.

Instead of getting into position to watch the solar eclipse, Iger was furiously working the phones from Italy to consummate a stunning event of his own -- a $12.5 billion sale of the Lakers seemingly out of nowhere, creating an eclipse unto itself across the worlds of sports and business.

Little did anyone know that these secret, cross-continental talks were about to put the Lakers in significant transition yet again -- with new owners evaluating everything and everyone; squabbling former owners, again, jostling for power and money; and an overhauled roster finally built in the image of its superstar, Luka Doncic.

Interviews with more than a dozen team insiders, league executives and others with intimate knowledge of the sale reveal how the deal, which was made over a furious 72 hours, upstaged an already-transformative offseason -- and reignited yet another unresolved round of messy public bickering among the six Buss siblings that still hangs uncomfortably over the beginning of this new season.

JUST A YEAR ago, Lakers governor Jeanie Buss had shocked the sports world by negotiating a sale to Walter after 46 years of family ownership. Though that deal was eventually approved by all six siblings, it was not a clean process.

According to several family sources, younger brothers Joey and Jesse Buss -- who, because of a "last-man standing" provision in Dr. Jerry Buss's family trust, were positioned to run the team one day after their older siblings died -- hadn't responded to the vote when the sale was initially announced.

If the family was going to sell, Joey and Jesse wanted to be a part of the process. They had recently pitched to the other siblings a way to do that -- albeit, sources with knowledge of the discussions said, at a lower valuation than the $10 billion their older sister subsequently agreed to in the deal with Walter. The younger Buss brothers eventually joined their four older siblings in voting for the sale to Walter, but the process created animosity.

Several siblings grumbled that Jeanie had not opened the bidding to outside buyers and had, instead, negotiated directly with Walter, multiple family sources said.

Walter, who already owned 27% of the Lakers, had the right of first refusal on any eventual sale of the Buss family's remaining shares, but how did anyone know how much the team would've fetched without actually putting it on the open market?

The relationship between Jeanie and her siblings disintegrated further when the Lakers, with Jeanie's approval, fired Janie, Joey and Jesse from their respective positions with the franchise within two months of closing on the sale.

All three had expected they'd keep their roles for at least some time while Jeanie was still the controlling owner, multiple family sources said.

The deal with Walter included contractual language to keep Jeanie in charge for the next five seasons but contained no such protections for any other family members.

Janie told ESPN's Baxter Holmes last season that her sister's actions had made her feel disrespected, like a "crumpled-up piece of paper thrown into the trash." She cited the desires of their father, who had purchased the Lakers in 1979 and died in 2013.

"I don't think my dad would be happy with the way things just went down," Janie told Holmes. "Not at all."

There was even more consternation, those sources said, when the Buss family members were suddenly charged more for hospitality and their tickets to Lakers games, shortly before the start of the playoffs as part of a larger restructuring of Lakers business practices.

That familial tension simmered throughout last season -- and came to a boil once again this summer.

FOR MUCH OF 2026, Iger and Kushner had been leading a group bidding for the potential Las Vegas NBA expansion franchise, which the NBA initially projected to go for $6-8 billion, according to industry and ownership sources.

But those bids had blown by that threshold, those sources said, and were approaching the then-record $10 billion valuation of Walter's sale.

Whichever group won the expansion bid would likely then need to spend what multiple sources estimated would be an additional $2 billion -- at least -- to build an arena in Las Vegas.

The Kushner-Iger group had been regarded as one of the favorites to land the team. Iger has had a longtime business relationship with NBA commissioner Adam Silver, from Iger's days negotiating broadcast rights deals for ABC/ESPN with the NBA. In 2020, the two collaborated with the NBPA to create "the bubble" at the Walt Disney Resorts in Orlando, Florida, where the NBA finished its season amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Iger had also been a longtime season-ticket holder of the LA Clippers, although he notably canceled them last season over the team's treatment of Chris Paul, a close friend of Iger's, sources close to him said.

Other finalists for the Las Vegas expansion franchise included groups headed by Walmart heiress Nancy Walton Laurie and her husband Bill Laurie; Las Vegas Golden Knights owner Bill Foley and former Phoenix Suns CEO Jerry Colangelo; and Canadian businessman Steve Apostolopoulos and former Milwaukee Bucks owner Marc Lasry.

As the Aug. 10 deadline for bids approached, Kushner and Iger discussed their options.

Over the past two decades, the 41-year-old Kushner had made a fortune building his private equity fund, Thrive Capital, with investments in technology companies such as Instagram, Spotify, Twitch, Stripe and OpenAI. This year, Kushner started a new fund, Thrive Eternal, as a hedge against artificial intelligence.

"These are assets with qualities that cannot be replicated by technology," Thrive Eternal says on its website. "Iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience. In a world shaped by abundant intelligence where creation scales and distribution fragments, we believe they will matter even more."

An expansion team is not exactly an iconic brand or a legacy franchise. The Lakers, New York Knicks, Chicago Bulls and Boston Celtics are. None of those was known to be for sale, however. The Knicks had just won an NBA title. The Celtics and Lakers had recently been sold to new owners for record amounts. The Bulls were firmly in the hands of the Reinsdorf family, who have not shown any interest in selling.

Still, Kushner and Iger kicked around the idea.

Would any of the owners of those franchises take a phone call or listen to an offer? How much would it take to pique their interest?

It was a bold, risky pivot to even make calls while they were in the throes of the expansion process. If word got out that they were considering moving away from the expansion franchise, would it risk their standing with the NBA?

Whatever they did would need to be quick -- and quiet.

WALTER WAS ON a ranch with spotty cell phone service on Aug. 9, when he got a call from a friend, asking whether he'd consider selling the Lakers, according to three sources with knowledge of his whereabouts and thinking.

The first conversation was short. The Lakers weren't for sale, Walter told his friend, who relayed the message to Kushner and Iger. But the two businessmen had reason to persevere in their efforts.

Two days earlier, on Aug. 7, they had called a well-connected financial industry source who was close enough to Walter to suggest he might be looking to restructure some of his business assets amid federal investigations of alleged fraud within his sprawling $365 billion financial empire, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the conversations.

They figured it was worth dropping a line in the water, baiting the hook at a number that would make him think about it.

The only catch was they needed an answer within 24 hours. There was no time for a long negotiation or intermediaries.

Kushner made the next call to Walter, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiation, and Kushner offered to buy Walter's shares at a $12.5 billion valuation -- a 25% increase in 14 months.

It was the kind of staggering "Godfather offer" Walter had presented to Jeanie Buss when he convinced her to sell him the majority of her family's shares a year earlier.

Walter decided to cut short his weekend trip and get to a place with better cell phone reception. They had his attention. By Monday, he had returned to his estate in White Oak, Florida.

He called his wife, Kimbra, and daughter, Samantha, and asked what they thought of him selling the Lakers.

He outlined the enormous return he'd make at this valuation -- nearly $4 billion because he had bought the first 27% of his Lakers shares at a $5 billion valuation in 2021 -- and the benefits that liquidity could provide him, given the remediation plans he had proposed to state insurance regulators.

Neither his wife nor daughter had an issue with him selling the Lakers, those sources said. They had been involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers for 14 years, but their attachment to the Lakers was still new.

After Walter's family signed off, the circle of people involved in the negotiations widened.

Advisers on both sides were sworn to secrecy. There wasn't time for Kushner and Iger's group to do anything resembling due diligence. They were buying the brand, as is, with as quick a close as you'll ever see in a $12.5 billion deal.

By the evening of Aug. 11 -- 72 hours after the idea had first been presented to him -- Walter had come to an agreement with Iger and Kushner.

JEANIE BUSS LEARNED of Walter's agreement to sell his shares of the Lakers hours before ESPN reported the news on the morning of Aug. 12, according to multiple sources with knowledge of their conversations.

She was stunned, according to sources close to her.

This was not what she had planned for or expected when she reached out to Walter in 2021 to suggest he purchase Philip Anschutz's shares to become the largest minority shareholder in the franchise, and with it, hold the first right of refusal to buy the Buss family's shares for a controlling interest in the team.

Walter and Buss had built a relationship over many years before he expressed an interest in buying into the Lakers.

Over the decade he owned the Dodgers, Walter had actively built bridges between L.A.'s premier baseball team and its basketball team. Lakers legend Magic Johnson was part of Walter's ownership group. Dodgers players were often invited to and hosted at Lakers games, and vice versa. Walter often attended games with Buss, while Buss attended Dodgers games with Walter.

At the time he bought Anschutz's shares, only people very close to the situation understood why it was so significant. Buss had essentially chosen Walter as her successor. Whenever she was ready to sell her family's controlling shares, he would have the inside track to buy them.

Buss chose Walter, multiple sources close to her said, because of how he owned and operated the Dodgers and the positive reviews he had gotten from associates of hers, including Johnson, tennis legend Billie Jean King and longtime Dodgers executive Lon Rosen. She had compared him to her father, Dr. Jerry Buss, for his commitment to winning publicly and privately over the years.

To those close to the situation, the question wasn't whether the Buss family would eventually sell to Walter but when. Older brothers Johnny and Jim had wanted to sell the team for years.

Jeanie, her sister Janie and younger brothers Joey and Jesse still had roles with the team and wanted to stay on longer.

In 2025, Walter came up with an offer he thought would make everyone happy: a $10 billion valuation -- generating approximately $800 million for each sibling -- and an agreement for Jeanie to stay on as controlling owner for five years, codified in writing as part of the agreement.

"Over the past decade, I have come to know Mark well -- first as a businessman, then as a friend and now as a colleague," Jeanie Buss said in a statement after the sale. "He has demonstrated time and time again his commitment to bringing championships to Los Angeles, and, on behalf of Lakers fans everywhere, I am beyond excited about what our future has in store."

Buss even showed that paperwork to Doncic and his team, his manager Lara Beth Seager said, to reassure them that she would still have final say over his basketball future.

Doncic had learned the hard way how an ownership change could affect him after his shocking trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Lakers in February 2025.

Former Mavericks owner Mark Cuban also thought he'd be allowed to stay on as head of basketball operations when he sold his controlling stake to the Adelson family in 2023. Cuban swore to Doncic that he wanted him to be a Maverick for life, but wasn't involved or included in the trade discussions that sent Doncic to L.A.

This time, it was Jeanie who would learn the hard way -- that whatever relationship she had built with Walter and others would be superseded by the harsh realities of the modern business world.

DESPITE THAT RELATIONSHIP, the man Jeanie chose as the next steward of the Lakers was not the rock-solid titan of the financial industry he appeared to be.

Walter, the public would soon learn, was under multiple federal criminal investigations before his purchase of the Lakers became official at the end of October. According to the Wall Street Journal, the FBI on Sept. 18, 2025, conducted a raid of a private plane at Chicago's Midway Airport, where Walter had been traveling, and seized a laptop and mobile phone.

Just 10 months later, Walter flipped the Lakers like a cold asset, not a crown-jewel, generational investment.

After five decades of family ownership, Jeanie had relinquished control of her family's most prized possession to someone who had treated it no differently than any other line item in his massive portfolio.

"I mean, he made $2.5 billion in 10 months by flipping the Lakers like a spec house," one family confidant said. "But that wasn't supposed to be the deal. Jeanie picked him because he was going to own it like he's owned the Dodgers."

Walter has not spoken publicly about the sale outside of an initial statement he released to ESPN.

In late August, his company, The Walter Group, issued a statement asserting it had been subjected to "multipronged attacks" from "unnamed sources with self-serving interests."

The statement said that TWG and its Group 1001 insurance companies had presented a plan to state insurance regulators to address regulatory concerns over a percentage of affiliated transactions it had misreported in its filings. TWG explained that the affiliated transactions in question are "common across the insurance industry" and "suggestions that TWG is looting insurers is defamatory and false."

Investigators are still looking into the company's dealings as it makes changes in the way it operates. TWG Global announced in late August that it had swapped out $6.5 billion of its assets to replace the type of affiliated loans regulators had taken issue with. The dual sales of the Lakers and Walter's minority 12.8% stake in Premier League club Chelsea have raised additional capital, while also leading to an assortment of buyers inquiring about the availability of the Dodgers and Los Angeles Sparks.

The company has emphatically denied that it is looking to sell its sports assets at "fire sale" prices to raise capital for its insurance operations. The sales of the Lakers and Chelsea came in at significant valuations -- a record in the case of the Lakers. However, sources with knowledge of the situation confirm a Bloomberg report that acknowledged there have been early-stage discussions about the Sparks at what would be a similarly massive valuation, estimated at $700 million.

Inquiries for the Dodgers have thus far been rebuffed, those sources said.

IGER LANDED BACK home in Los Angeles a few days after the sale agreement was reached. The first visitor he entertained at his house was Jeanie Buss, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the meeting.

He had given public comments to the California Post immediately after news of the sale broke that the new ownership group intended to honor the agreement Buss had with Walter to stay on as controlling owner, but added, "if something changes, then it changes."

Despite the public hedge, Iger reaffirmed his commitment to Jeanie to maintain a role after the sale closes when they met, those sources said. They have stayed in regular contact since then.

Whether she'll be able to do so -- and what that role ultimately is -- depends on how the latest round of family discord is resolved.

By the time Walter decided to sell his stake in the Lakers in mid-August, family sources said there had already been renewed calls among the siblings to sell the remaining 17.8% of the team that the family owned.

The Lakers had fired four of her siblings already. Jim Buss, who was fired in 2017, noted to the group that there was little justification for keeping the family's remaining shares, other than nostalgia and Jeanie keeping her controlling-ownership power for four additional years, according to multiple family sources. He circulated a proposal he hoped would satisfy all parties.

On the night of Aug. 10, two days before the sale, Lakers vice president of finance Joe McCormack called for a meeting of the Buss siblings to discuss a dissolution of the family trust and seek approval to lock down all family shares for four years under a new trust, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin.

When the family discussed McCormack's proposal on Aug. 11, no mention was made of Walter's impending sale to Kushner and Iger. The family woke up to the news of the massive sale the following morning like everyone else.

On Aug. 17, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Johnny, Jim, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss had voted to sell the remaining family shares to Iger and Kushner, using "go-along" rights they had been given as part of the sale to Walter. (Technically, those rights can be only invoked once Walter officially notifies the family that he has signed a deal to sell, which hasn't happened yet.)

Jeanie was the only family member who did not vote to sell. In fact, she did not even respond to the vote that had been called a week earlier.

Later that day, her lawyer, Adam Streisand, sent a letter to the five siblings, challenging the legality of their vote based on a 2017 court order that required the two co-trustees, Janie and Joey, to always vote to ensure she remained the controlling owner of the team.

The siblings immediately responded to Streisand's initial letter with a statement of their own, reaffirming their desire to sell. They contended they needed only a majority (four of six votes and two of three co-trustees) to enact that go-along provision, according to sources with knowledge of the siblings' position.

Jeanie currently controls the Buss family trust, which owns 17.8% of the Lakers. NBA rules mandate that a controlling owner must own at least 15% of the team. An alternate governor must own at least 5%.

Still, multiple family sources said there have been settlement talks between the two sides over the past two months.

Each sibling stands to make an additional $371 million if the family sells the entirety of its shares via the go-along provision.

The siblings could also try to find a buyer at a higher valuation, a possibility fueled by a pitch, which The Wall Street Journal obtained, to Thrive Eternal investors in which the company projected the Lakers valuation to be at least $30 billion within a decade.

The dispute spilled back into the public on Oct. 7, when the five siblings formally filed a response to Jeanie's suit.

"Jimmy, Johnny, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss, the five of six siblings who voted to sell the Trust's shares in the Lakers, today filed their formal opposition, demonstrating that Jeanie Buss's petition is legally and factually baseless," the siblings said in a statement issued to ESPN.

"While discussions among the siblings continue, their focus remains on facilitating the proposed transaction and the [Buss family] trust's participation in it, while ensuring that all beneficiaries, including Jeanie, are treated equally."

Nine days later, the five siblings submitted, on behalf of Joey and Janie, an additional filing, this one challenging Jeanie and her previous petition that seeks to remove them as co-trustees and void the siblings' 5-1 vote to sell the family's remaining stake in the team.

Through it all, the foundation of the dispute remains the same: whether the five siblings can sell their share of the team without Jeanie's approval.

A court date is set for Dec. 8 if no settlement is reached.

DONCIC WAS THE only person outside of the small circle of people close to Walter, Kushner and Iger who had any inkling how the sports world was about to dramatically change before Aug. 12.

The last time he had gotten a text from Seager, his longtime manager, at an odd hour was in February 2025, when she reached him after midnight and told him he had been traded to the Lakers.

This time, she had gotten a tip well after midnight at her home in Dallas that something big might be happening again. She texted Doncic, who was just waking up in Slovenia, alerting him to the possibility.

All summer, they had been planning a five-day team bonding retreat in Doncic's home country for his new Lakers teammates. On the first night, they'd all eat at his favorite restaurant, Cubo, in his hometown of Ljubljana.

Then, they'd play golf some 40 miles north on the perfectly manicured grounds of Royal Bled, sitting in a valley beneath the tree-lined peaks of the Alps. Another day was built around rowing lessons on Lake Bled, taught by Slovenian Olympian Jani Klemencic. Three high-speed boats, 15 Lakers, learning to row together.

Then, in one early-morning text, all those plans seemed secondary.

It was a stunning turn with no forewarning. Just a week earlier, Seager had met Jeanie and Rosen for dinner. Nothing had seemed amiss. At that point, Kushner had yet to engage Walter about the possibility of buying the Lakers.

Doncic had developed a good relationship with Walter and Jeanie Buss in the 18 months since he had come to Los Angeles, meeting and texting with both of them regularly. Walter even took him and a group of teammates to a Backstreet Boys concert at The Sphere in Las Vegas last summer, after Doncic agreed to a three-year, $165 million contract extension with the Lakers.

If the sale goes through and Kushner and Iger are approved by the NBA, and that is expected to happen by the end of the year or early next year, according to multiple sources close to the sale process, they'd be his fifth team owners across two franchises in the past three years.

By the time Seager called Doncic to tell him the deal was done, he had already processed the initial shock.

"There's not much that can shock me anymore," Doncic told her.

The next day, as he congratulated the new owners, he acknowledged the seismic move and posted on X:

"I've gotten used to big changes over these last few years."

stories.headline: Alex Iwobi equals Mohamed Salah's Premier League appearance mark, closes in on Toure's
stories.summary: Nigeria midfielder Alex Iwobi has drawn level with Egypt's Mohamed Salah as the African player with the second-most appearances in Premier League history, a mark that puts the Nigerian just 25 games short of holder Kolo Toure.
stories.body:
Nigeria midfielder Alex Iwobi has drawn level with Egypt's Mohamed Salah as the African player with the second-most appearances in Premier League history, a mark that puts the Nigerian just 25 games short of holder Kolo Toure.

The 30-year-old made his 328th appearance in Fulham's 1-0 victory at Coventry City on Saturday. Only former Ivory Coast defender Toure, who played 353 times for Arsenal, Manchester City and Liverpool, has made more appearances among African internationals.

Already Nigeria's leading appearance-maker in the league, Iwobi needs another 26 games to take the African record outright.

His latest outing came a week before the 11th anniversary of his Premier League debut, when he came off the bench for Arsenal in a 3-0 victory at Swansea City on October 31 of 2015. He scored on his first league start the following March, helping Arsenal beat Everton 2-0 at Goodison Park.

Everton became his next club in 2019, before he returned to London to join Fulham in September 2023, where he has since passed Shola Ameobi's Nigerian appearance record of 298 games.

Iwobi's landmark Premier League appearance was acknowledged by the NFF, with acting general secretary Emmanuel Ikpeme identifying Toure's mark as the next target.

"The NFF celebrates Alex Iwobi for this new achievement and we wish him even greater glory," Ikpeme said in a federation statement.

"We will be very happy to see him become the African with the most appearances in the Premier League in the near future."

Oscar Bobb scored Fulham's winner against Coventry, securing a second successive 1-0 league victory following last weekend's win over Hull City, with Iwobi himself scoring the decisive goal in that game.

The appearance standings place Iwobi ahead of several of African football's longest-serving Premier League players. Ghana's Jordan Ayew and Ivory Coast's Wilfried Zaha have 305 appearances each, while Ameobi's 298 put the former Newcastle United and Crystal Palace forward sixth among African internationals.

Among Nigerians, Nwankwo Kanu finished with 273 appearances, followed by Yakubu Aiyegbeni with 252 and John Mikel Obi with 249. Defender Joseph Yobo played 228 times across spells with Everton and Norwich City.

Yobo's contribution also included an endurance mark that no other Nigerian has hit. The former Super Eagles captain played every minute of all 38 Premier League matches for Everton during the 2006-07 season, completing 3,420 minutes as the club finished sixth. He started every game and was neither substituted nor sent off during the league campaign.

Iwobi also holds Nigeria's Premier League assists record, having overtaken Kanu's total of 29 in 2024. Yakubu remains Nigeria's leading Premier League scorer, with 95 goals in 252 appearances. His goals came for Portsmouth, Middlesbrough, Everton and Blackburn Rovers.

Another Nigerian, Efan Ekoku, holds a place in the competition's history becoming the first player to score four goals in a Premier League match when Norwich won 5-1 at Everton on September 25 of 1993.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Bruins-Canes highlights another massive night of games
stories.summary: Here's what you need to know about all 11 games on the NHL calendar on Tuesday.
stories.body:
After Tuesday's games, a full four weeks of the 2026-27 NHL season will be in the books.

There have been plenty of shocks and surprises, and the schedule of games coming up promises even more.

It's not surprising that the Hurricanes are in first place in the Metro; it's quite a bit surprising is that the Bruins are tops in the Atlantic. Those two teams meet in Tuesday's marquee matchup (8 p.m. ET, ESPN), but there's 10 other games to monitor too.

Here's a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Columbus Blue Jackets at Philadelphia Flyers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CBJ -115, O/U: 5.5

Speaking of surprises, no one predicted that these two teams would be bringing up the rear in the Metro at this juncture, but here we are. (The Blue Jackets do get a little grace, as they've played just nine games so far for some reason.)

Philly has been the beneficiary of a recent heater by Matvei Michkov, and he now leads the team in points (eight goals, two assists). Columbus enters this game having won an overtime thriller over Vegas in its last game, with Adam Fantilli notching the game-winner. Which young star shines brightest on Tuesday?

Boston Bruins at Carolina Hurricanes

8 p.m. ET (ESPN) | CAR -192, O/U: 6.5

These two franchises have had quite a history, going back to 1979-80 when the Canes were still the Hartford Whalers.

Overall, the B's hold a 115-80-24 record against Hartford/Carolina in the regular season, and a 26-16 edge in the postseason.

More recently, the Bruins won in the 2019 conference finals and the 2020 first round, while the Canes won a first-round matchup in 2022.

From a stats perspective, both teams have a player in the top 10 in scoring (Sebastian Aho, David Pastrnak) as well as save percentage (Pyotr Kochetkov, Jeremy Swayman).

Los Angeles Kings at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | LA -118, O/U: 5.5

Both teams enter this matchup thankful that the Canucks exist, as Vancouver is keeping them out of the NHL's basement. But on a personal note, it's a reunion of sorts with former linemates Artemi Panarin and Patrick Kane (who played together in Chicago in 2015-16 and '16-17, as well as New York in spring of 2023).

The Blackhawks got a Connor Bedard bump upon the captain's return -- winning two games in a row -- before losing the next three. L.A. won two in a row before losing to a Devils team that was fired up about acquiring Connor Hellebuyck the day prior.

Montreal Canadiens at St. Louis Blues

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | STL -118, O/U: 6.5

The Canadiens continue to be without leading scorer (and captain) Nick Suzuki, as he recovers from an upper-body injury. Goaltender Jacob Fowler continued his breakout campaign, backstopping the Habs to a 2-1 win in the Heritage Classic on Sunday night.

On the other side, the Blues have gone undefeated against Canadian teams so far, winning 7-2 against the Senators and 2-1 against the Jets. Will they make it 3-0?

New York Islanders at Nashville Predators

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NSH -118, O/U: 5.5

The Preds have a formula for success this season: when scoring three or more goals this season, they've gone 2-0-1. The issue here is that they'll be welcoming one of the NHL's stingiest defensive teams to Bridgestone Arena. Thanks to Ilya Sorokin -- and a strong defensive structure -- the Isles have allowed just 2.55 goals per game, which is fifth fewest in the league. Which side blinks first?

New Jersey Devils at Dallas Stars

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | DAL -142, O/U: 5.5

It's probably too soon to expect newest Devil Connor Hellebuyck to be between the pipes for this showdown.

But for fans of elite netminding, may we interest you in some Jake Oettinger? The Stars' franchise tender has a 6-2-1 record, with a 1.43 goals-against average and .930 save percentage.

Both teams come in to this matchup hot, as the Devils have won five of their last six and the Stars have won all five of their last five.

Florida Panthers at Winnipeg Jets

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -130, O/U: 5.5

It's rare that a pair of interconference opponents play two games against one another so close on the calendar, but that's exactly what's happening this week for the Panthers and Jets. After this matchup Tuesday, they'll play again in Sunrise on Friday.

Given the tight proximity between matchups, might there be some message-sending or tone-setting in this one?

Minnesota Wild at Utah Mammoth

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | UTA -142, O/U: 6.5

There's no clearer way to set the stakes here: the winner of this game will be in first place in the Central Division after four weeks. Most expected the Wild to be one of the Central powerhouses again, but the Mammoth have arrived ahead of schedule.

On an individual basis, it's worth mentioning Kirill Kaprizov, who has 13 goals this month. That is three off of the record for goals in a single October, held by Mario Lemieux. On the Utah side, Clayton Keller's 15 points through 12 games put him on pace for 105 points, which would be a career high and make him the first triple-digit scorer in franchise history.

Ottawa Senators at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -162, O/U: 6.5

Has the rest of the NHL figured out the Golden Knights? Vegas enters this game on a three-game losing streak, though they remain in second place in the Pacific Division thanks to an 8-2-0 start. The Sens have been on opposite sides of lopsided affairs the past three games -- a 5-1 win over the Panthers, then a 6-2 loss to the Sharks, then a 7-4 win over the Rangers.

Which team's superstar will reign supreme on Tuesday? Ottawa's Tim Stutzle has 16 points through 12 games, while Vegas' Jack Eichel has 19 through 13.

Vancouver Canucks at Anaheim Ducks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | ANA -198, O/U: 6.5

The popular internet phrase is "I just hope both teams have fun." Well, based on the goals-against average of these clubs, it looks like they will! The Canucks enter the contest with an NHL-worst 4.62 goals allowed per game, while the Ducks aren't much better, sitting 24th with 3.36.

And if you like how the game goes Tuesday, these two will match up again on Tuesday Nov. 3 as well.

Buffalo Sabres at San Jose Sharks

10:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | BUF -135, O/U: 6.5

The Sabres ended the longest postseason drought in the NHL last season, returning to the Stanley Cup playoffs after 14 seasons out. The Sharks haven't gone that long without a playoff berth, but they are hoping to end their seven-year drought with a return this spring.

The player to watch here, as always with the Sharks, is Macklin Celebrini. Despite missing two games, the EA Sports cover athlete leads the team in scoring (five goals, 10 assists), six points clear of second place.

Buffalo has been led by breakout winger Jack Quinn, who has 11 points in 11 games, well ahead of his career-high pace of 51 points from last season.

As for recent history, these two teams split the 2025-26 season series, with the home team winning each game.

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.
